# Ethical Food Guide: full content

Everything in the guide at https://ethicalfood.biblioverse.org/ as plain Markdown. Content updated 2026-11-14.

Being listed is not an endorsement: companies are not assessed one by one, and some are diversified groups that also sell animal products.

## Organizations

https://ethicalfood.biblioverse.org/organizations.html

### Nonprofit and advocacy

- **The Good Food Institute** (United States, 2016): Global nonprofit working on open-access research, policy and industry support across plant-based, cultivated and fermentation proteins. <https://gfi.org>
- **The Good Food Institute Brasil** (Brazil): Brazilian arm of GFI. Publishes the cultivated meat glossary and the map of the Brazilian sector. <https://gfi.org.br>
- **Cellular Agriculture Australia** (Australia): Sector body for Australia. Author of the Key Terms language guide used on this site. <https://www.cellularagricultureaustralia.org>
- **Cellular Agriculture Canada** (Canada, 2019): Community and advocacy group for Canadian cellular agriculture. <https://www.cellularagriculture.ca>
- **Food Frontier** (Australia): Think tank speeding up alternative protein markets in Australia and New Zealand. Now joining forces with Cellular Agriculture Australia. <https://www.foodfrontier.org>
- **Modern Agriculture Foundation** (Israel, 2014): Israeli nonprofit building an alternative protein ecosystem. <https://modern-agriculture.org>
- **ProVeg International** (Germany, 2017): Food awareness organization working with governments and companies. Also runs the ProVeg Incubator. <https://proveg.com>
- **The Vegan Society** (United Kingdom, 1944): The original vegan organization, which also coined the word vegan. <https://www.vegansociety.com>
- **Vegan France** (France, 2013): French organization promoting vegan food. <https://vegan-france.fr>
- **Roślinnie Jemy** (Poland): Polish campaign promoting plant-based eating. <https://roslinniejemy.org>
- **Sweet Farm** (United States, 2015): California farm sanctuary and regenerative agriculture nonprofit. <https://sweetfarm.org>

### Research and think tanks

- **New Harvest** (United States, 2004): Field-building organization advancing cellular agriculture for the public good, through open research funding. <https://www.new-harvest.org>
- **Kind Earth Tech** (United States, 2018): Foundation behind the KET food maps of the alternative protein industry. <https://www.kindearth.tech>
- **World Resources Institute** (United States, 1982): Global research organization. Publishes analyses on shifting diets and sustainable food. <https://www.wri.org>
- **Sentience Institute** (United States, 2017): Think tank studying moral circle expansion and the end of animal farming. <https://www.sentienceinstitute.org>
- **Shojinmeat Project** (Japan, 2014): Japanese citizen-science project on do-it-yourself cell culture. <https://shojinmeat.com>
- **Centro Nacional de Tecnología y Seguridad Alimentaria** (Spain, 1981): Spanish food technology and safety research center. <https://www.cnta.es>
- **DIL German Institute of Food Technologies** (Germany, 1983): German applied research institute on food technology, including proteins. <https://www.dil-ev.de>
- **Food Innovation Australia** (Australia, 2013): Australian food and agribusiness growth center. <https://www.fial.com.au>

### Trade associations

- **Plant Based Foods Association** (United States, 2016): US trade association for plant-based food companies. <https://www.plantbasedfoods.org>
- **Plant Based Foods of Canada** (Canada, 2018): Trade association for Canadian plant-based food companies. <https://plantbasedfoodscanada.ca>
- **European Vegetable Protein Association** (Belgium, 1977): European trade body for vegetable protein producers. <https://www.euvepro.eu>

### Investor networks

- **FAIRR Initiative** (United Kingdom, 2015): Investor network on the risks and opportunities of intensive livestock and protein. <https://www.fairr.org>

### Education

- **Cellular Agriculture Society** (United States, 2018): Nonprofit focused on education and on the textbook Modern Meat. <https://www.cellag.org>
- **Future Food Institute** (Italy, 2014): Italian institute for food innovation education and research. <https://futurefoodinstitute.org>
- **UFMG Alt Protein Project** (Brazil): Student group at the Federal University of Minas Gerais. <https://www.instagram.com/ufmgaltprotein/>

### Data and maps

- **New Protein** (United States): Collection of industry landscape maps covering alternative protein, milk, cheese, algae and fungi. <https://newprotein.org>
- **Protein Report** (United States): Reporting and data on alternative protein funding. <https://www.proteinreport.org>
- **Protein Directory**: Online directory of protein industry players. <https://proteindirectory.com>

### Universities

- **Maastricht University** (Netherlands, 1976): Home of Mark Post, who presented the first cultivated hamburger in 2013. <https://www.maastrichtuniversity.nl>
- **Wageningen University & Research** (Netherlands, 1918): Leading agri-food university, with research on plant-based meat structure. <https://www.wur.nl/en>
- **Technion** (Israel, 1912): Israeli institute where Shulamit Levenberg’s tissue engineering research led to Aleph Farms. <https://www.technion.ac.il/en/>
- **Hebrew University of Jerusalem** (Israel, 1925): Research by Yaakov Nahmias here led to Future Meat, now Believer. <https://en.huji.ac.il>
- **Tel Aviv University** (Israel, 1956): Israeli research university listed in the project spreadsheet. <https://english.tau.ac.il>
- **University of Bath** (United Kingdom, 1966): UK research on tissue engineering and scaffolds for cultivated meat. <https://www.bath.ac.uk>
- **National University of Singapore** (Singapore, 1905): Research university in one of the first countries to approve cultivated meat. <https://nus.edu.sg>
- **Nanyang Technological University** (Singapore, 1981): Singaporean research university with food science programs. <https://www.ntu.edu.sg>
- **University of Melbourne** (Australia, 1853): Australian research university listed in the project spreadsheet. <https://www.unimelb.edu.au>
- **University of Toronto** (Canada, 1827): Canadian research university listed in the project spreadsheet. <https://www.utoronto.ca>
- **North Carolina State University** (United States, 1887): US land-grant university listed in the project spreadsheet. <https://www.ncsu.edu>
- **Worcester Polytechnic Institute** (United States, 1865): US institute listed in the project spreadsheet for bioengineering research. <https://www.wpi.edu>
- **Kent State University** (United States, 1910): US research university listed in the project spreadsheet. <https://www.kent.edu>
- **CEFET-MG** (Brazil, 1909): Brazilian federal technology education center in Minas Gerais. <https://www.cefetmg.br>

## Reasons to consider cellular agriculture

https://ethicalfood.biblioverse.org/reasons.html

A summary in our own words of "90 Reasons to Consider Cellular Agriculture" by Kristopher Gasteratos (2019), with the original numbering. These are 2019 projections of the technology’s potential, not measured results; later life cycle assessments show that impact depends heavily on energy source and scale.

### Health and food safety

1. **No pathogen contamination**: Monitored production with little human handling should lower the risk of Salmonella or E. coli reaching food.
2. **Lower famine risk**: Food supply depends less on livestock and can continue through events that would otherwise stop harvests.
3. **No fecal contamination**: Most fecal contamination happens at slaughter. Removing slaughter removes that route; a 2015 Consumer Reports test found fecal-indicator bacteria in all beef sampled.
4. **No added hormones**: Growth hormones used to speed up animal growth would not be needed.
5. **Longer shelf life**: Cleaner production could keep food safe for longer.
6. **Feeding the future**: An added supply route for animal products as the population approaches 10 billion by 2050.
7. **No swine or avian flu**: Without farmed animals, this source of zoonotic outbreaks goes away.
8. **Geographic independence**: Regions with poor access to animal products could make them locally.
9. **Natural disasters**: Animals left behind in floods can contaminate water supplies, as happened after Hurricane Florence. No livestock, no such risk.
10. **Heme iron without animals**: People with iron-deficiency conditions who avoid animal products would gain another source of heme iron.
11. **No botulism from carcasses**: Not handling slaughtered animals reduces this route of infection.
12. **Man-made disasters**: Land-based production sidesteps contamination of seafood by events such as oil spills.
13. **Safe food in a catastrophe**: Secure cell banks could provide radiation-free food after a nuclear war or major impact.
14. **No antibiotics in food**: The process is not expected to rely on the antibiotics used in animal farming.
15. **Fewer superbugs**: Less antibiotic use by the animal protein sector means less pressure toward resistance.
16. **Healthier foods**: Nutrition could be tuned, for example with less fat and more protein.
17. **No plastic in seafood**: Fish that never swam in the sea do not ingest ocean plastic.
18. **No mercury in seafood**: Seafood made without catching fish avoids mercury accumulation.
19. **Safer vegetables**: Livestock runoff can contaminate nearby crops, as in a Romaine lettuce recall linked to a cattle farm.
20. **Options for restricted diets**: People who avoid animal products but are allergic to soy, nuts or gluten would have more choices.
21. **Biomedical spillovers**: Advances could carry over to regenerative medicine and other fields.
22. **Whey without cows**: Athletes who only use plant protein could have an animal-free whey.
23. **Prion monitoring**: Monitored systems can screen for prions, helping avoid outbreaks like mad cow disease.
24. **Hypoallergenic milk**: Dairy could be made suitable for people with milk allergies, especially children.
25. **Better taste**: Control over nutritional profiles could also improve flavor.

### Environment: land

26. **Cattle: 99% less land**: Estimated land saving for beef.
27. **Dairy: 97% less land**: Estimated land saving for dairy.
28. **Poultry: 66% less land**: Estimated land saving for poultry.
29. **Pigs: 82% less land**: Estimated land saving for pork.
30. **Seafood: 55% less land**: Estimated land saving for seafood.
31. **Overall: 80% less land**: Estimated land saving across products.

### Environment: water

32. **Cattle: 98% less water**: Estimated water saving for beef.
33. **Dairy: 99.6% less water**: Estimated water saving for dairy.
34. **Poultry: 92% less water**: Estimated water saving for poultry.
35. **Pigs: 95% less water**: Estimated water saving for pork.
36. **Seafood: 86% less water**: Estimated water saving for seafood.
37. **Overall: 94% less water**: Estimated water saving across products.

### Environment: greenhouse gases

38. **Cattle: 96% less GHG**: Estimated emissions cut for beef.
39. **Dairy: 65% less GHG**: Estimated emissions cut for dairy.
40. **Poultry: 74% less GHG**: Estimated emissions cut for poultry.
41. **Pigs: 85% less GHG**: Estimated emissions cut for pork.
42. **Seafood: 59% less GHG**: Estimated emissions cut for seafood.
43. **Overall: 76% less GHG**: Estimated emissions cut across products.

### Environment: ecosystems

44. **45% less energy**: Estimated energy saving for meat. Later studies show this depends heavily on the energy source.
45. **Less animal waste on land**: No livestock means none of the 1.75 billion tons of manure that pollute groundwater.
46. **Less animal waste at sea**: Less farm runoff means fewer dead zones and algal blooms.
47. **No bottom trawling**: Seafood without nets dragged across the seabed, which destroys old coral.
48. **No fish blood discharge**: Aquaculture would no longer release virus-carrying blood into public waters.
49. **Fewer pesticides**: Less feed-crop runoff of pesticides and herbicides into oceans.
50. **Less transport pollution**: Local production can shorten land and sea freight.
51. **Fewer fishing fleets**: Local production reduces polluting fleets.
52. **Less deforestation**: Lower grain demand removes a major pressure on forests and leaves room to reforest.
53. **A plastic alternative**: Cell-grown rhino horn (keratin) could replace some plastics.
54. **Less ocean plastic**: Fishing gear is a large share of plastic in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch (46% in one study).

### Human and animal rights

55. **Safer jobs**: Less exposure to the injury and amputation risks of industrial meat work.
56. **Lower psychological harm**: Workers avoid the trauma, including PTSD, linked to repeated slaughter.
57. **Fewer recall costs**: Fewer cullings and contamination recalls paid for with public money.
58. **Safer than tanneries**: Cell-grown leather avoids toxic tannery exposures linked to long-term illness.
59. **Less seafood fraud**: Tighter control reduces mislabeling, which one survey put at 1 in 3 fish.
60. **No forced labor at sea**: Production without fishing fleets removes the setting for forced labor in that industry.
61. **Cheaper food**: The source expects prices to keep falling. This remains unproven at scale.
62. **An end to killing for food**: Over a trillion animals, most of them fish, are killed for food each year. This removes the need.
63. **Less animal suffering**: An alternative to factory farming that needs no animals to be raised.
64. **Less poaching**: Cell-grown ivory or rhino horn may undercut the market for poached products.
65. **Pet food**: An alternative for owners who do not want to feed their pets conventional animal products.
66. **Less overfishing**: Seafood demand can be met without taking fish from threatened ecosystems.
67. **No bycatch**: No nets means no dolphins and turtles caught by accident.
68. **Protecting endangered species**: Species targeted directly, such as sharks for fin soup, face less pressure.
69. **Less biodiversity loss**: Less farmland expansion means less habitat loss.
70. **Grain for people**: Grain from poorer countries would no longer be shipped to feed factory-farmed animals.
71. **Environmental justice**: Low-income communities near livestock operations would be spared manure spraying and its health effects.
72. **Less wildlife hunting**: Products such as bear gallbladder could be made without hunting.

### Business and economics

73. **Financial security**: Fewer shocks from food scandals, disasters and costly recalls.
74. **Carbon tax exposure**: Lower-impact products would be less exposed to future carbon pricing.
75. **Product consistency**: Tighter process control gives more consistent output and less fraud.
76. **Welfare premium**: Consumers who pay more for high-welfare products may pay for this too.
77. **Independent of climate**: Production can run in hot or cold regions alike.
78. **Property values**: Homes near intensive livestock facilities lose value, by up to 88% at very close range, per the sources cited.
79. **No surplus buying**: Less need for public purchases of surplus, such as the US$20 million of US cheese in 2016.
80. **Domestic production**: Land-constrained nations such as Singapore and Japan could produce at home.
81. **Byproduct supply**: By-products such as horn could also be grown if farmed supply falls.
82. **Fewer bailouts**: Less need for government safety nets for dairy farmers.
83. **New jobs**: A new industry creates biotech and agricultural jobs.
84. **Less dairy waste**: Better control of output means less wasted dairy.

### Future and beyond

85. **Food on Mars**: A more sustainable way to feed long missions and future settlements.
86. **Personal production**: Home devices could one day let people make custom products.
87. **New animal foods**: A wider range of products, including species no longer farmed or even extinct.
88. **Astronaut health**: Diet could be adjusted to conditions such as muscle atrophy in space.
89. **Food safety in space**: Tightly controlled environments lower pathogen exposure on missions.
90. **New materials**: Biomaterials could offer strength and toughness for demanding uses.

## Books, reports and articles

https://ethicalfood.biblioverse.org/books.html

### Food system and technology

- **Regenesis**, George Monbiot (2022): Argues for shrinking farmland and for microbial protein.
- **Sixty Harvests Left**, Philip Lymbery (2022): Soil, industrial farming and what food could look like instead.
- **Animal, Vegetable, Junk**, Mark Bittman (2021): History of how the food system was shaped by industry.
- **Billion Dollar Burger**, Chase Purdy (2020): Reporting on the race to bring cultivated meat to market.
- **Meat Planet**, Benjamin Aldes Wurgaft (2019): An anthropologist’s critical look at the promises of cultured meat.
- **The End of Animal Farming**, Jacy Reese Anthis (2018): How scientists, entrepreneurs and activists could build an animal-free food system.
- **Clean Meat**, Paul Shapiro (2018): Journalistic account of the early cultivated meat companies and the people behind them.
- **Farmageddon**, Philip Lymbery, Isabel Oakeshott (2014): Investigation into the true costs of cheap meat.

### Textbooks and science

- **Cultivated Meat: Technologies, Commercialization and Challenges**, Springer (2024): Technical overview from the laboratory to industrial scale. <https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-55968-6>
- **Cultivated Meat to Secure Our Future**, Michel Vandenbosch, Philip Lymbery (eds.) (2024): Essay collection on the case for cultivated meat. <https://www.new-harvest.org/blog/cultivated-meat-to-secure-our-future-new-book-open-access-chapter>
- **Modern Meat**, Cellular Agriculture Society (2021): Textbook on cultivated meat with over 100 contributors.

### Reports and guides

- **Media Guide: How to talk about cellular agriculture**, Cellular Agriculture Australia (2024): Guidance for journalists. <https://assets-global.website-files.com/641400f02d9306cbd4fb3f94/6614cde01226b58d37bee299_Cellular%20Agriculture%20Australia%20-%20Media%20Guide%20V1.0%20(1).pdf>
- **Plano de Ensino para Disciplinas em Proteínas Alternativas**, The Good Food Institute Brasil (2023): Conceptual model for university courses. <https://gfi.org.br/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Plano-de-Ensino-para-Disciplinas-em-Proteinas-Alternativas-Modelo-Conceitual.pdf>
- **Mapa do Setor de Proteínas Alternativas**, The Good Food Institute Brasil (2023): Map of the sector in Brazil. <https://gfi.org.br/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Mapa-do-Setor-de-Proteinas-Alternativas_GFI-Brasil.pdf>
- **Key Terms in Cellular Agriculture**, Cellular Agriculture Australia (2023): Language guide with preferred and non-preferred terms. <https://assets-global.website-files.com/641400f02d9306cbd4fb3f94/65659be903ceedf3aaedc231_Language%20Guide%20V1.0.docx%20(1).pdf>
- **Glossário de Carne Cultivada**, The Good Food Institute Brasil (2020): Bilingual technical glossary, Portuguese and English. <https://gfi.org.br/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/Glossario-Carne-Cultivada_GFI-Brasil.pdf>
- **Meat: the Future series. Alternative Proteins**, World Economic Forum, Oxford Martin School (University of Oxford) (2019): Argues that North American and European levels of meat consumption, extended to 10 billion people, are incompatible with the UN climate and environment goals, and maps the protein alternatives. <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lGiWZYxTaVJRGWpuhsWLxa1ACIPphhMq/view>
- **Formulating With Animal-Free Ingredients**, Institute of Food Technologists (2019): Practical notes on formulation. <https://gfi.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/IFTJune2019Animalfreeformulations.pdf>
- **90 Reasons to Consider Cellular Agriculture**, Kristopher Gasteratos (2019): The source of this site’s Reasons page. <http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:38573490>

### Articles

- **A carne já é muito barata, ao contrário do que pensam**, Julio Cesar Prava (2024): Opinion piece, in Portuguese: animal products are artificially cheap, because their price leaves out subsidies, environmental damage and the suffering of animals. <https://juliocesar.medium.com/a-carne-j%C3%A1-%C3%A9-muito-barata-ao-contr%C3%A1rio-do-que-pensam-47fd77a0dd94>
- **10 motivos pelos quais a carne cultivada deve superar a carne tradicional**, Julio Cesar Prava (2023): Opinion piece, in Portuguese, on why cultivated meat should overtake traditional meat. <https://juliocesar.medium.com/10-motivos-pelos-quais-a-carne-cultivada-deve-superar-a-carne-tradicional-568963bd638a>
- **Ex-ante life cycle assessment of commercial-scale cultivated meat production in 2030**, Pelle Sinke et al. (International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment) (2023): Projects the 2030 footprint, which depends heavily on using renewable energy. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-022-02128-8>
- **Rapid global phaseout of animal agriculture has the potential to stabilize greenhouse gas levels**, Michael Eisen, Patrick Brown (PLOS Climate) (2022): Models the climate effect of phasing out animal farming. One of the authors founded Impossible Foods. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pclm.0000010>
- **Projected environmental benefits of replacing beef with microbial protein**, Florian Humpenöder et al. (Nature) (2022): Replacing 20% of beef with microbial protein by 2050 could halve deforestation and related emissions. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04629-w>
- **Scale-up economics for cultured meat**, David Humbird (Biotechnology and Bioengineering) (2021): Critical techno-economic analysis of the cost of producing at scale. <https://doi.org/10.1002/bit.27848>
- **Global food system emissions could preclude achieving the 1.5° and 2°C climate change targets**, Michael Clark et al. (Science) (2020): Shows that food emissions alone could put the climate targets out of reach, even if fossil fuels stopped. <https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aba7357>
- **The carbon opportunity cost of animal-sourced food production on land**, Matthew Hayek et al. (Nature Sustainability) (2020): Estimates how much carbon could be removed if land used for animal food returned to native vegetation. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-020-00603-4>
- **Plant-based and cell-based approaches to meat production**, Natalie Rubio, Ning Xiang, David Kaplan (Nature Communications) (2020): Compares the science and challenges of the two main routes. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20061-y>
- **Food in the Anthropocene: the EAT–Lancet Commission**, Walter Willett et al. (The Lancet) (2019): Proposes a planetary health diet for feeding 10 billion people within environmental limits. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31788-4>
- **Reducing food’s environmental impacts through producers and consumers**, Joseph Poore, Thomas Nemecek (Science) (2018): Data from about 38,000 farms: one of the most cited comparisons of the environmental impact of foods. <https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaq0216>
- **The biomass distribution on Earth**, Yinon Bar-On, Rob Phillips, Ron Milo (PNAS) (2018): The census of life on Earth, which found that livestock far outweigh wild mammals. <https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1711842115>
- **Bringing cultured meat to market: Technical, socio-political, and regulatory challenges in cellular agriculture**, Neil Stephens et al. (Trends in Food Science & Technology) (2018): Overview of what stands between the science and the shelf. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tifs.2018.04.010>
- **Anticipatory life cycle analysis of in vitro biomass cultivation for cultured meat production in the United States**, Carolyn Mattick et al. (Environmental Science & Technology) (2015): A skeptical counterpoint: projects high energy use, comparable to or above some farmed meats. <https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5b01614>
- **Cultured meat from stem cells: Challenges and prospects**, Mark Post (Meat Science) (2012): Early roadmap by the scientist who presented the first cultivated hamburger in 2013. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.meatsci.2012.04.008>
- **Environmental impacts of cultured meat production**, Hanna Tuomisto, M. Joost Teixeira de Mattos (Environmental Science & Technology) (2011): The first widely cited estimate of the footprint of cultured meat. <https://doi.org/10.1021/es200130u>

## Glossary

https://ethicalfood.biblioverse.org/glossary.html

### Sector

- **Alternative protein** (Proteína alternativa): Protein made from plants, by fermentation or by growing cells, rather than from raised animals.
- **Cellular agriculture** (Agricultura celular): Umbrella term for using cells and related technologies to make ingredients, food and other farm products. Not a synonym for cell cultivation.
- **Cultivated meat** (Carne cultivada): Meat made by growing animal cells directly. The term preferred by the sector.
- **Factory farming** (Pecuária industrial): Intensive animal production at industrial scale.
- **Food manufacturing facility** (Instalação de produção de alimentos): The regulated plant where final products are made. The sector prefers this to "lab".
- **Hybrid product** (Produto híbrido): A food combining sources, such as cultivated cells with plant protein.
- **Life cycle assessment (LCA)** (Avaliação do ciclo de vida (ACV)): Method for estimating a product’s environmental impact from inputs to disposal.
- **Plant-based** (À base de plantas): Made from plants and formulated to replace an animal product.

### Technologies

- **3D bioprinting** (Bioimpressão 3D): Depositing cells and materials in layers to build a tissue structure.
- **Biomass fermentation** (Fermentação de biomassa): Growing fast-growing microorganisms, such as fungi, for their protein-rich mass, which is the food itself.
- **Bioprocess** (Bioprocesso): The sequence of steps that uses living cells to make a product at scale.
- **Cell cultivation** (Cultivo celular): Taking cells from an animal or plant and giving them the nutrients and conditions to multiply and mature into tissue.
- **Extrusion** (Extrusão): Pressing and heating plant protein to give it a fibrous, meat-like texture.
- **Gas fermentation** (Fermentação gasosa): Fermentation in which microorganisms are fed gases such as CO₂ along with nutrients.
- **Molecular farming** (Agricultura molecular): Engineering plants to produce a target ingredient, which is then extracted and purified.
- **Precision fermentation** (Fermentação de precisão): Using microorganisms such as yeast to produce a specific functional ingredient, often by inserting the gene for it. Long used for rennet and insulin.
- **Scale-up** (Escalonamento): Moving a process from small volumes to industrial production.
- **Tissue engineering** (Engenharia de tecidos): Combining cells, scaffolds and signals to build functional tissue.
- **Traditional fermentation** (Fermentação tradicional): Using microbes to change the flavor or texture of ingredients, as in tempeh.

### Cells and organisms

- **Adipocyte** (Adipócito): Fat cell, important to the flavor and texture of meat.
- **Biopsy** (Biópsia): Removing a small tissue sample, a common way of obtaining starter cells.
- **Cell bank** (Banco de células): A stored, characterized stock of cells used to start production.
- **Cell line** (Linhagem celular): A population of cells that can be kept growing in culture.
- **Differentiation** (Diferenciação): The process in which a cell becomes a specialized type, such as muscle.
- **Fibroblast** (Fibroblasto): Cell that makes connective tissue and the extracellular matrix.
- **Host strain** (Cepa hospedeira): The microorganism engineered to make the target molecule in precision fermentation.
- **Immortalization** (Imortalização): Changing cells so that they keep dividing beyond their normal limit.
- **Mycelium** (Micélio): The root-like network of threads of a fungus.
- **Mycoprotein** (Micoproteína): Protein-rich food made from fungal biomass.
- **Myoblast** (Mioblasto): Precursor cell that fuses with others to form muscle fibers.
- **Pluripotent stem cell** (Célula-tronco pluripotente): Stem cell able to become almost any type of cell in the body.
- **Proliferation** (Proliferação): The phase in which cells multiply in number.
- **Satellite cell** (Célula satélite): Muscle stem cell, widely used as a starting point for cultivated meat.
- **Senescence** (Senescência): The point at which cells permanently stop dividing.
- **Stem cell** (Célula-tronco): Unspecialized cell that can renew itself and turn into other cell types.

### Culture media

- **Amino acid** (Aminoácido): Building block of proteins and a key ingredient of culture media.
- **Culture medium** (Meio de cultura): The nutrient liquid in which cells grow, usually the largest cost in cultivated meat.
- **Feedstock** (Matéria-prima): Raw material that feeds a fermentation or culture, such as sugars.
- **Fetal bovine serum (FBS)** (Soro fetal bovino (SFB)): Serum from calf fetuses, historically used in cell culture. The sector is working to replace it.
- **Growth factor** (Fator de crescimento): Signaling protein that tells cells to grow or differentiate.
- **Hydrolysate** (Hidrolisado): Protein broken into smaller pieces, used as a low-cost nutrient source.
- **Serum-free medium** (Meio sem soro): Culture medium made without animal serum.

### Scaffolds

- **Biomaterial** (Biomaterial): Material designed to interact with living cells, as in scaffolds.
- **Decellularization** (Descelularização): Removing cells from a tissue, such as a plant, to reuse its structure.
- **Extracellular matrix (ECM)** (Matriz extracelular (MEC)): The network of proteins and sugars around cells in tissue.
- **Hydrogel** (Hidrogel): Water-rich polymer gel used to hold cells.
- **Microcarrier** (Microcarreador): Tiny bead that gives adherent cells a surface to grow on in a bioreactor.
- **Scaffold** (Suporte (scaffold)): A structure that supports cells and gives tissue its shape.

### Bioreactors and process

- **Bioreactor** (Biorreator): The vessel that gives cells or microbes controlled conditions to grow.
- **Contamination** (Contaminação): Unwanted microbes entering a culture, a key operational risk.
- **Downstream processing** (Processamento a jusante): The steps after growth that harvest and purify the product.
- **Fed-batch** (Batelada alimentada): Adding nutrients during a run without removing the culture.
- **Perfusion** (Perfusão): Continuously replacing medium while keeping cells in the reactor.
- **Shear stress** (Tensão de cisalhamento): Force from moving fluid, which can damage cells.
- **Stirred-tank bioreactor** (Biorreator de tanque agitado): Common bioreactor design that mixes contents with an impeller.

### Market and regulation

- **Analog** (Análogo): A product designed to replace a specific animal product.
- **B2B / B2C** (B2B / B2C): Selling to other businesses, or directly to consumers.
- **Contract manufacturer** (Fabricante terceirizado): A company that makes products for other brands.
- **GRAS** (GRAS): "Generally recognized as safe", a US food ingredient status.
- **Novel food** (Novo alimento): A regulatory category for foods without a history of consumption, such as in the EU.
- **Price parity** (Paridade de preço): When a new product costs the same as the conventional one.

### How to talk about it

- Prefer **Cultivated meat**, avoid *Lab-grown, in vitro, test-tube, vat-grown*: Sounds unnatural and is inaccurate: final products are made in food plants.
- Prefer **Cultivated meat**, avoid *Synthetic meat*: Too broad, with negative connotations.
- Prefer **Cultivated meat**, avoid *Slaughter-free, cruelty-free*: Value-laden and derogatory to traditional producers.
- Prefer **Cultivated meat**, avoid *Fake meat, frankenmeat, schmeat*: Derogatory and not descriptive.
- Prefer **Cultivated meat**, avoid *Clean meat*: Value-laden, and does not distinguish it from plant-based meat.
- Prefer **Cellular agriculture**, avoid *Cell-based food production*: Too narrow: not all products are food or animal-derived.
- Prefer **Precision-fermented**, avoid *Acellular*: Not widely understood.
- Prefer **Functionally equivalent**, avoid *Nature-identical, dairy-identical*: "Identical" is not technically accurate and may carry legal risk.

Using our proprietary oil-structuring technology, we produce fats with up to 40% fewer calories and up to 80% less saturated fat than conventional options such as butter and margarine.
